title: Gesture drawing and the line of action
summary: Gesture drawing records the movement and weight of a pose in a few flowing marks before any anatomy or outline. You learn to find the line of action, see the figure as three tilting masses (head, ribcage, pelvis), and tell rhythm (curves) from tension (angles). Everything else in this group sits on top of this skill.
learning_outcomes: Find the single dominant line of action in a photo or live pose and draw it in one stroke.
Describe any pose as three masses (head, ribcage, pelvis) with different tilts, then link them with limbs that flow from those masses.
Tell a rhythm pose (curves) from a tension pose (zigzags and corners) and pick marks to match.
Say what separates gesture from outline and from detail.

resources.title: How to Draw Gesture (free lesson in Figure Drawing Fundamentals)
resources.free_notes: This lesson is marked free on its own page (9:31 there; the course page lists 16:17, so the free and premium cuts may differ). The parent course, Figure Drawing Fundamentals, is $150 one-time (57 lessons, 16h44m). Only four gesture lessons are visibly free: this one, Gesture Step by Step, the 2-Minute Poses assignment examples and the Gesture critique. The 30-second-poses lesson and every later section (Bean, Structure, Landmarks, Robo Bean, Mannequinization, Balance, Exaggeration, Proportions, Measuring, Shading) are premium.
resources.notes: Watch this first, then 'How to Draw Gesture - Step by Step' (27:38, also free: https://www.proko.com/course-lesson/how-to-draw-gesture-step-by-step). Covers gesture as the flow linking forms, C/S/I curves, the longest axis of each body part, rhythm versus tension, asymmetry and exaggeration. Pause and copy the demo marks.

resources.title: Free drawing tutorial: gesture and pose basics
resources.free_notes: The page calls this roughly 15-minute hands-on tutorial free (line of action, three movable masses, limb placement). The same site also sells memberships and photo bundles, so only the tutorial is confirmed free.
resources.notes: Do it right after the Proko lesson: it is a different explanation of the same idea (three movable masses and limb placement) and gives instant practice poses.

resources.title: The Gesture Course (free lessons)
resources.free_notes: Course is $125 one-time (27 lessons, 11h16m). The page says 5 lessons are free; I could confirm 3: How to Think About Gesture (26:05), How to Draw Expressive Hands (17:14, lesson 17) and How to Draw Expressive Feet (16:02, lesson 18). The 16-line method for difficult poses, foreshortening, weight and balance and the shape method are in the premium part.
resources.notes: Take the free first lesson, 'How to Think About Gesture' (26:05), for a more theoretical view of why gesture comes before structure. Skip the rest unless you decide to buy the course.

resources.title: Simplified Gesture and Structure with Steve Huston (free lesson)
resources.free_notes: Marked free (20:48), lesson 128 of 185 in the Drawing Basics course, which is $159 one-time; the rest of the course is mostly premium (the course page says 58 free lessons, but only six were visible to me).
resources.notes: Watch after you have done a week of gesture drills. Huston shows how to combine gesture with simple structure using curves and corners, which is where this module hands over to the construction module.

practice.title: Single-line warm-up
practice.description: For each reference pose draw only the main curve of the action, then add one line for the ribcage tilt and one for the pelvis tilt. Nothing else.

practice.title: Three-mass thumbnails
practice.description: Reduce each pose to a head shape, a ribcage shape and a pelvis shape, tilted as in the reference, joined by the line of action. Check that ribcage and pelvis lean in different directions.

practice.title: Rhythm or tension sort
practice.description: Before drawing, label each reference 'curves' or 'angles'. Then draw it using marks that match the label. Compare your label with a friend or with your own second look.
practice.dose: 10 curve poses and 10 angle poses, 1 minute each

practice.title: Limbs flow from the masses
practice.description: Add arms and legs as continuous lines that start inside the torso masses instead of being stuck on afterwards.

practice.title: Overlay check
practice.description: On tracing paper or a digital layer, draw the line of action directly over the reference photo, then over your drawing. Note where yours is straighter, shorter or more symmetrical.
practice.dose: 10 minutes at the end of each session

done_when: You can point to the line of action in a new reference within about 5 seconds and an overlay confirms it.
Your 1-minute sketches show whether the figure is leaning, reaching, twisting or sitting without any detail.
Ribcage and pelvis are drawn at clearly different angles in most of your sketches.
You can explain in one sentence why gesture is not an outline.
common_mistakes: Tracing the outline of the body instead of the movement through it.
Drawing symmetrical, upright poses because they feel safe.
Starting with the head and adding limbs as separate sticks, so nothing flows.
Adding detail (faces, fingers) in a 1-minute drawing.

title: Timed gesture practice progression (30 seconds to 5 minutes) and session review
summary: A repeatable session that climbs from 30-second poses to 5-minute ones, plus a short review routine so the practice actually changes your drawings. The ladder shows what each time slot should and should not contain. The review step is the part most self-taught students skip.
learning_outcomes: Run a 30-minute timed session without fiddling with tools.
Know what each time slot is for: 30 s action only, 1 min masses, 2 min limbs and weight, 5 min first structure.
Review a session by naming your two most frequent errors and one thing to try next time.
Keep a log you can compare across weeks.

resources.free_notes: Marked free (37:58) inside Figure Drawing Fundamentals ($150). The matching 30-second poses lesson (4:54) is not marked free. The critique 'Figure Drawing Critiques - Gesture' (1:00:31) is also free: https://www.proko.com/course-lesson/figure-drawing-critiques-gesture
resources.notes: Watch a few student examples, then the critique to learn how a teacher reviews a gesture sheet: what is praised, what is flagged (stiffness, symmetry, lost line of action). Use those criteria in your own review step.

resources.title: Proko Timer (reference packs with a session timer)
resources.free_notes: Free: sample packs such as '300 Best Of 2025 Free Sample Pack' (300 images), 'Classical Art Poses: Free Sample Pack' (439) and 'Grafit Reference Sampler' (81). The page shows Log In and Sign Up and a sessions history link, but does not say whether an account is needed to start. Licence terms are not shown on the page; the page's robots tag includes NoAI.
resources.notes: Pick the free sample packs and set the image count and seconds per image. Useful if you want to build the exact 30 s, 1 min, 2 min, 5 min ladder as separate sessions.

practice.title: The 29-minute ladder
practice.description: Ten poses at 30 s, six at 1 min, four at 2 min, two at 5 min. Spend the 30 s poses on action only, 1 min on three masses, 2 min on limbs and weight, 5 min on first structure.
practice.dose: 29 minutes, 3 times a week for 4 weeks

practice.title: Review ritual
practice.description: Lay the sheet out. Circle your best and worst pose. Write one sentence about each. Name the error that appears most often, and write one change for next session.

practice.title: Memory replay
practice.description: The next day, redraw from memory the pose you found hardest. Then check against the reference.
practice.dose: 2 minutes, once a day on session days

practice.title: One-lens sessions
practice.description: Run a whole session looking at only one thing: line of action, then silhouette, then weight on the supporting leg, then overlaps.

practice.title: Same pose, three times
practice.description: Draw one pose at 30 s, 2 min and 5 min on one page. Write what the extra time added and what it cost you.

done_when: You have logged at least 12 sessions with a written review for each.
Your 30-second drawings read as poses and your 5-minute ones add structure without losing the action.
You can name your two most common errors from your own notes, not from guesswork.
You can set up a session in under 2 minutes.
common_mistakes: Using extra seconds to polish details instead of fixing the action.
Skipping the review so the same errors repeat for months.
Staring at the paper; most of the time should be spent looking at the reference.
Picking only easy standing poses; include twisting, sitting and foreshortened ones.

title: Simplified figure construction: mannequin, bean and ribcage-pelvis, boxes and cylinders
summary: Construction turns the gesture into a set of simple volumes you can rotate in your head: ribcage and pelvis as eggs, beans or boxes, limbs as tapered tubes, joints as balls. You practise building a mannequin on top of a gesture line and checking that it holds up from other angles. Free video here is thin, so the core path mixes two free lessons with a public-domain book.
learning_outcomes: Build a standing or leaning figure from gesture line, ribcage, pelvis, limbs and joints in about 5 minutes.
Keep ribcage and pelvis volumes consistent in 3/4 and side views.
Draw limbs as tubes with overlapping forms and cross-contours.
Explain how construction differs from gesture and when to use each.

resources.title: Simplified Gesture and Structure with Steve Huston (free lesson)
resources.free_notes: Marked free (20:48), lesson 128 of 185 in the Drawing Basics course, which is $159 one-time; the rest of the course is mostly premium (the course page says 58 free lessons, but only six were visible to me).
resources.notes: Start here. Huston adds simple structure (tubes, curves and corners) to a gesture. Redraw his demo with your own reference before moving on.

resources.title: Introduction to Figure Construction (2 free lessons)
resources.free_notes: $125 one-time, 48 lessons, 10h53m; also listed on Gumroad at $125 as a recording of his university lectures. Only two lessons are free: What Are the Fundamentals? (11:09) and Foundations (19:46). Sections that matter later (Proportions, Hand Construction, Foot Construction, Dynamic Poses, Foreshortening, Gesture, Rendering) are premium.
resources.notes: Watch the two free lessons, 'What Are the Fundamentals?' and 'Foundations', for a university-style view of the shapes you need before building a figure. The remaining 46 lessons are paid.

resources.title: Constructive Anatomy (1920)
resources.free_notes: Archive.org shows 'Free Download, Borrow, and Streaming' (PDF and EPUB) for the 1920 Pelham, N.Y. edition and no rights statement. A 1920 US publication is public domain in the US; DrawingBooks.org states all its books are public domain in the US and shows the same book page by page at https://www.drawingbooks.org/bridgman1/index.html. Do not confuse it with Bridgman's later 1950s guides, which I did not check. The book contains anatomical drawings of nude figures.
resources.notes: Read 'General Anatomy' and 'Masses and Movements of the Body' (book pages 11-17) in the online reader at https://www.drawingbooks.org/bridgman1/index.html and copy two of the mass diagrams. The style is dated (blocky wedges), but it is the origin of many modern mannequins.

resources.title: Constructive Figure Drawing I (7 weeks)
resources.free_notes: 15h58m in total; price not shown on the page I could read. Every lesson shows a Preview link but the page does not say whether previews are free. Week 1 Gesture and Structure is 1h30m49s; Week 2 Form and Position is 2h9m2s; Week 3 Head and Torso, Week 4 Shoulders and Limbs, Week 5 Proportions and the Whole Figure.
resources.notes: Use as the paid next step if you want a full structured course after the free material. It follows the same order as this module and the next three.

practice.title: Bean or box torsos
practice.description: Draw the ribcage as an egg or box and the pelvis as a bean or box, tilted against each other, with a centre line wrapping around both. Add the spine as a curve between them.

practice.title: Tube limbs
practice.description: Fill a page with tapered arm and leg tubes bending in space. Add cross-contour lines that curve around the tube and ellipses at the joints.

practice.title: One pose, four cameras
practice.description: Pose a 3D figure, then draw it from four camera angles. Keep the mannequin proportions consistent.

practice.title: Mannequin over photo
practice.description: Draw the gesture line, then the mannequin, next to a reference photo. Afterwards overlay the mannequin on the photo and check where joints land.

practice.title: Copy a mass diagram
practice.description: Redraw two of Bridgman's body-mass diagrams from the free scan, then redraw them from memory the next day.

done_when: You can build a standing mannequin in 5 minutes that reads as a body from front and 3/4 views.
Ribcage and pelvis stay the same size and shape as you rotate them across poses.
Limbs overlap with clear in-front and behind relationships.
You can tell when a drawing has gesture but no structure, or the reverse, and fix it.
common_mistakes: Treating the mannequin as a rigid robot and losing the gesture.
Drawing the ribcage too small, which shortens the torso and makes arms look long.
Using flat circles for joints instead of volumes that overlap.
Starting the mannequin without a line of action.

title: Figure proportion systems and variation: heads-tall canons, children, body types and ages
summary: Heads-tall canons (7, 7.5, 8 heads) give you landmarks to check against, but real people vary and children are built differently. This module teaches the canon first, then uses reference to draw different ages, builds and heights. Free structured video is limited here; the free route uses public-domain texts plus photo and 3D references.
learning_outcomes: Lay out a standing figure at a chosen heads-tall height with landmarks (chin, nipples, navel, crotch, knees) placed in the right zones.
Describe how a young child's head, torso and limb ratios differ from an adult's.
Draw three clearly different body types without defaulting to one build.
Use a canon as a check and not as a rule.

resources.title: Figure Drawing (R. G. Hatton): 'Method and Proportion', then Head and Neck, Trunk, Limbs, Drapery
resources.free_notes: Site states its books are public domain in the US (its own claim). Presented as a two-page viewer. Contents: Method and Proportion (viewer page 1), The Head and Neck, The Trunk, The Upper Limb, The Lower Limb, Drapery. The page text does not describe the proportion chapter, so open it and judge; the language is early 20th century.
resources.notes: Read the first chapter for how the author divides the body, then compare his divisions with a modern 7.5 or 8-head chart. Copy his proportion diagram, then test it on photos.

resources.title: The Human Figure (J. H. Vanderpoel)
resources.free_notes: Page-by-page reader, about 168 pages, 17 chapters from eyes and head through trunk, limbs, hands and feet to The Figure as a Whole, with Student's Notes. Site claims US public domain; the page does not give a publication year (it dates to the early 1900s, from my own knowledge, not the page).
resources.notes: Read 'The Figure as a Whole' and the chapters on limbs for proportion and landmarks. Student's Notes give practical exercises.

resources.title: Figure Drawing Children (C. H. Rimmer)
resources.free_notes: Listed on DrawingBooks.org as public domain in the US (site claim). The landing page I could open showed only purchase links and a tip jar; I could not confirm the contents or page count, so open the reader and check.
resources.notes: For child proportions. If the reader does not load, use child and teen photos from Line of Action's age filter instead.

The Store menu shows Subscriptions, Pay as you go, photo bundles and gift cards, so there is a paid tier, but I could not read what the free tier limits (ads, photo counts, timer options). practice.title: Head-unit chart
practice.description: Draw one standing pose three times on equal head-unit grids at 7, 7.5 and 8 heads. Mark chin, nipples, navel, crotch, knees.

practice.title: Age ladder
practice.description: Pick a child, a teen, an adult and an older adult from reference. Mark head-count and the halfway point on each, then draw each as a simple mannequin.

practice.title: Body-type sheet
practice.description: Choose six reference photos of different builds. For each, draw only the ribcage-to-pelvis-to-limb length ratios as a stick diagram.

practice.title: Landmark ruler
practice.description: Mark eye line, chin, nipples, navel, crotch and knees on five standing photos. Compare them against your canon and write the differences.

practice.title: Exaggerate on purpose
practice.description: Redraw one pose at 6 heads and at 9 heads to see how height changes the read of the character.

done_when: You can lay out a standing figure at a chosen height with landmarks in about 2 minutes.
You can say how a young child's proportions differ from an adult's and draw both.
You have drawn at least three distinct body types from reference.
You treat the canon as a check and can say where reality differs.
common_mistakes: Applying one adult canon to every body, so children look like small adults.
Measuring heads-tall from the wrong baseline (e.g. including hair or a raised heel).
Using 9-10 head fashion proportions for realistic figures.
Forgetting that foreshortening changes apparent proportions.

title: Skeleton and muscle anatomy by region: torso, arms, legs, and surface landmarks
summary: Anatomy gives your construction a reason: where bones show under skin, which muscles bulge in which poses, and how parts attach. The free route uses Proko's 115 free anatomy lessons, a free 3D atlas to rotate every layer, and a short public-domain primer. Study by region and always draw, never just read.
learning_outcomes: Draw ribcage, pelvis, spine and shoulder girdle from memory in simplified form from three angles.
Name and place at least 12 surface landmarks (e.g. collarbone ends, elbow points, kneecap, front hip bones).
Block in the major muscle groups of torso, upper arm and thigh as simple masses with the right attachments.
Use anatomy to explain a bulge or dip in a reference pose.

resources.title: Anatomy of the Human Body (115 free lessons)
resources.free_notes: 371 lessons, about 77 hours, three parts: Torso (163 lessons, 59 free), Arms (101, 28 free) and Legs (107, 28 free). Full course listed at about $434 (parts about $145-159 each) on 2026-10-13. Free lessons I could name: Introduction to Human Anatomy for Artists (14:49), How to Do an Anatomy Tracing (14:31), The Language of Anatomy (6:59), The 6 Types of Joints (12:06), Simplifying Joints in Perspective Assignment Example 2 (4:02), Anatomy Critiques Types of Joints (1:16:41), How to Draw Hand Bones (8:17) and How to Draw Feet (14:23). Premium examples: foreshortened hands, female hands. The page does not name the other free Arms and Legs lessons. Anatomical figures are nude.
resources.notes: Start with the free Basics: Introduction to Human Anatomy for Artists, How to Do an Anatomy Tracing, The Language of Anatomy, The 6 Types of Joints. Then work through the free Torso lessons (59), then Arms (28), then Legs (28). The lesson hrefs are on https://www.proko.com/course-lesson/introduction-to-human-anatomy-for-artists and similar. Do the anatomy tracing exercise for each region.

resources.title: Z-Anatomy: free layered 3D atlas of the human body
resources.credit: Gauthier Kervyn (design, modelling, anatomy), Marcin Zielinski (script), Lluis Vinent (Unity)
resources.free_notes: Source repository states code and content are CC BY-SA 4.0 (attribute and share alike). It is a Blender template with skeleton, muscle, vessel, nerve and organ layers, built on BodyParts3D, with a male body and Terminologia Anatomica labels. A 2022 CG Channel article says the Blender file and an Android app are free and points to https://www.z-anatomy.com, which loads an in-browser viewer. The models are unclothed anatomical figures. Wikipedia-derived definitions may contain errors, per the project.
resources.notes: Use it as the 3D lab: switch on bones only, then add muscle layers, and rotate to see the part you just studied from the front, side and back. Sketch the region at three angles.

resources.title: Artistic Anatomy of the Human Figure (Henry Warren)
resources.free_notes: Online reader, about 64 pages (inferred from the page menu). Contents: The Skeleton; Head and Neck; Muscles of the Face and Neck; The Shoulder Joint, Trunk and Back; The Arm (front, back, side); The Legs and their muscles. Site claims US public domain. Illustrations are old engravings of nude anatomical figures.
resources.notes: A fast written summary to read next to the Proko lessons. Copy one plate per region.

resources.title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e (textbook)
resources.free_notes: Page says the book can be read online or downloaded free. The licence is not shown in the text I could read, but OpenStax publishes under open licences, so confirm on the page. Medical, not artist-oriented: use it to check names, attachments and movement, not for drawing method.
resources.notes: Use the skeletal system and muscular system chapters to check names and attachments (chapter numbers not read; I believe they are chapters 6-8 and 11, check before relying on that). Not for drawing method.

practice.title: Anatomy tracing
practice.description: Trace a bone or muscle diagram, naming landmarks as you go. One region at a time (spine and ribcage, pelvis, shoulder, arm, leg). Then redraw it without tracing.
practice.dose: 5 traces per region, about 15 minutes each

practice.title: Landmark hunt
practice.description: On three photos of different people, mark 10 bony landmarks. Check them against the 3D atlas.

practice.title: Bones in the pose
practice.description: Take six gesture sketches you have already made and draw the simplified skeleton inside them.

practice.title: Muscle block-ins
practice.description: For torso, upper arm and thigh, draw the main muscle groups as simple shapes, with arrows showing direction.

practice.title: Atlas rotation
practice.description: Pick a region in Z-Anatomy or in the browser-based BodyParts3D viewer (Japan's Database Center for Life Science; filter to Bone or Muscle), sketch it from three angles, then check each against the others.

practice.title: Memory test
practice.description: Without a reference, draw ribcage, pelvis and spine. Check, mark errors, redraw. Repeat weekly.

done_when: You can draw the ribcage, pelvis and spine in side, front and 3/4 view from memory.
You can name and place 12 or more surface landmarks on a living reference.
You can block in torso, upper arm and thigh muscles correctly in at least two poses.
You use anatomy notes to explain, not to decorate, a drawing.
common_mistakes: Memorising Latin names without drawing the shapes.
Drawing detailed muscles on every figure, even when fat or clothes hide them.
Making left and right muscles identical and ignoring the pose.
Skipping bones and going straight to muscles.

title: Hands
summary: Hands are built from a flat wedge-shaped palm, a thumb that sits on its own base, and fingers that follow arcs. You learn to start from gesture and simple parts, then add bones, then foreshortening and holding objects. There are good free lessons and a free 1920 book of hand studies.
learning_outcomes: Draw a hand in about 20 seconds as a simple palm shape plus a thumb plane.
Show finger length relationships and knuckle arcs without measuring each time.
Draw a hand holding an object so the grip makes sense.
Draw 10 distinct hand poses from imagination that look plausible.

resources.title: How to Draw Expressive Hands (free lesson in The Gesture Course)
resources.free_notes: Marked free (17:14, lesson 17 of 27); the full Gesture Course is $125. Teaches hands as simple parts with shape, rhythm and expression for storytelling.
resources.notes: Watch, then redraw each of his hand examples once without tracing.

resources.title: How to Draw Hand Bones (free lesson in Anatomy of the Human Body)
resources.free_notes: Marked free (8:17, lesson 177 of 371); a premium version with more content exists. The full anatomy course is about $434. Covers carpals, metacarpals and phalanges and proportions by halving.
resources.notes: Do this after a week of gesture-first hands. Draw the bones, then draw a hand over them.

resources.title: Book of a Hundred Hands (1920)
resources.free_notes: Online reader to about page 175. Contents include bones of the wrist, fingers, knuckles, thumb, veins and muscle origin, insertion and action. Site states its books are public domain in the US (its own claim); 1920 publication supports that. The page also offers paid copies.
resources.notes: Use as a visual dictionary of hand poses and anatomy diagrams; copy ten plates over weeks.

practice.title: Foreshortened hands
practice.description: Draw hands pointing at you and palms toward you, using boxes and overlapping shapes.

done_when: You can draw a believable hand from any of the common angles in about a minute.
Finger lengths and knuckle arcs hold up when compared with a photo.
Grips look like they would hold an object.
You stop hiding hands in pockets or behind objects in your drawings.
common_mistakes: Drawing each finger as a separate sausage with no palm.
Making all fingers the same length and the palm flat.
Putting the thumb too high or too low on the palm.
Over-rendering one hand while the rest of the drawing stays rough.

title: Feet
summary: A foot is an arched wedge with a heel at the back and toes that fan out at the front; the ankle bones sit at different heights. Weight changes how the foot spreads and flattens. Two free lessons cover construction and gesture, and a free 1920 book covers the bones.
learning_outcomes: Draw a foot from side, front and 3/4 as a wedge with arch and toe groups.
Place the inner and outer ankle bones at their different heights.
Show whether a foot carries weight or is lifted.
Draw shoes over a foot form.

resources.title: How to Draw Feet (free lesson in Anatomy of the Human Body)

done_when: You can draw a foot from three angles without a reference and it reads as a foot.
Ankle bones are at different heights in your drawings.
A planted foot looks like it carries weight; a lifted foot looks relaxed.
Shoe drawings show the foot shape inside.
common_mistakes: Drawing a flat, shoe-shaped blob with no arch.
Making all toes equal sausages.
Placing both ankle bones at the same height.
Making feet too small relative to the head and leg.

title: Head construction: sphere-and-planes methods (Loomis-style, Reilly-style, block head)
summary: You build the head as a ball with the sides sliced off, then add a jaw and a centre line that wraps around the form, so the face can turn to any angle. Proko's free Loomis-method lessons cover the basic method. Reilly and block-head methods are mostly in paid courses.
learning_outcomes: Construct a head from front, side, 3/4, up-tilt and down-tilt using a sphere, centre line, brow line and jaw.
Place brow, nose and chin lines consistently.
Simplify the head into larger planes (block head) for lighting.
Explain the difference between a Loomis, Reilly and block-head approach.

practice.title: Loomis ball and planes
practice.description: Draw a ball, slice the sides, add centre line, brow line, nose line and chin line. Do it for front, side and 3/4.

practice.title: Tilt it
practice.description: Take one head and tilt it up, down and sideways; keep the construction lines wrapping.

practice.title: Block head
practice.description: Simplify to a box-and-planes head, marking which planes face up, front and side.

practice.title: Skull to head
practice.description: Draw a simple skull (cranium, cheekbones, jaw), then wrap a head around it.

practice.title: Memory heads
practice.description: Draw 10 heads from memory at random angles, then compare with a 3D head.

done_when: You can construct a head at six different angles in under 3 minutes each.
Brow, nose and chin lines stay consistent across a sheet.
Jaw and cheekbones read as volumes, not outlines.
You can draw a believable head from imagination.
common_mistakes: Drawing an egg instead of a ball with planes cut off.
Centre line that stays flat instead of wrapping around the form.
Ignoring the jaw and the back of the skull.
Placing eyes too high; they sit near the middle of the head.

title: Facial features and expressions
summary: Eyes, nose, mouth and ears are small forms wrapped around the head; expressions come from brow, eyelid, cheek and mouth shifts across the whole face. Free structured video is scarce for this topic, so the core path is a classic anatomy text, a free expression-reference tool, and Darwin's 1872 book. Paid NMA lessons are the fuller structured option.
learning_outcomes: Draw eye, nose, mouth and ear from front, 3/4 and side with correct construction.
Build six basic expressions on one head by changing brows, eyelids, cheeks and mouth.
Check an expression at thumbnail size.
Use a coding system (FACS action units) as a checklist for what changes in an expression.

practice.description: Draw an eyeball as a sphere with lids wrapping over it, from front, 3/4 and side.

practice.title: Nose and mouth planes
practice.description: Draw noses and mouths as simple planes from front, 3/4 and side.

practice.title: Ears
practice.description: Draw ears with their main folds simplified into one C shape and an inner Y shape.

practice.title: Expression grid
practice.description: On one head construction, change only brows, eyelids and mouth corners to produce six expressions. Use the FACS action-unit list (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_Action_Coding_System) as a checklist of what moves.

practice.title: Asymmetry drill
practice.description: Draw expressions where the two sides differ (smirk, sneer, wink).

practice.title: Photo expressions
practice.description: Pick a face reference tool and draw quick expressions to practise reading them.

done_when: You can draw each feature from three angles without reference.
You can produce six readable expressions on one head construction.

You can say which muscles or action units changed in an expression.

Treating expression as just mouth shape and forgetting brows, eyelids and cheeks.
Making expressions symmetrical.
Drawing the full iris in realistic eyes when the upper lid usually covers part of it.

title: Portrait drawing and likeness
summary: A likeness comes from getting the big proportions and shapes of one particular head right before adding any feature detail. You practise measuring on a photo, comparing with overlays, and building the head with Loomis-style construction first. Proko's portrait course and critique give the free core; NMA's likeness lesson is the paid deeper dive.
learning_outcomes: Capture a recognisable likeness from a photo in about 30 minutes.
Name the three proportions that make a given face different from the average.
Use a measure-and-compare routine to find errors before adding detail.
Keep a consistent head angle and lighting across a series of portraits.

practice.title: Three self-portraits
practice.description: Draw yourself three times: 20 minutes construction first; 40 minutes with measurements; then 20 minutes from memory followed by correction. Use a mirror or a photo.

practice.title: Proportion map
practice.description: Mark eye-to-eye, eye-to-nose, nose-to-mouth and face width on a photo. Redraw the face from the map before drawing features.

practice.title: Shape-first likeness
practice.description: For six strangers' photos, spend the first 5 minutes on hairline, jaw, brow and cheek planes only, then place features.

practice.title: Flip check
practice.description: Flip both the photo and the drawing horizontally every 10 minutes to see errors you had stopped seeing.

practice.title: Subtle caricature
practice.description: Push the three most distinctive proportions in a face by about 20% and compare with the photo.

practice.title: Master portrait copies
practice.description: Copy three portrait drawings from open-access collections.

done_when: A friend can recognise the subject from a 30-minute portrait.
You can name three proportions that set this face apart.
You have finished at least three self-portraits and compared them.
Your measuring routine catches errors before shading.
common_mistakes: Drawing features before the head shape.
Using wide-angle or very close photos, which distort faces.
Erasing and guessing instead of measuring.
Making faces more symmetrical than the real ones.

title: Hair
summary: Hair reads as a few large volumes with a growth direction, not as separate strands. You learn to block it as masses over the head construction, then add edge detail and light. There is one short free lesson, and open-access museum drawings give plenty of examples to copy.
learning_outcomes: Block hair as three to five 3D volumes over a head construction.
Show part, hairline and growth direction.
Draw at least four hair types (straight, wavy, curly, coily) with believable volume.
Add strands only at edges and accents.

resources.notes: Teaches hair as volumes rather than strands, so it looks three-dimensional instead of like spaghetti. Watch once, then draw along.

resources.notes: Pose the model, change hair, and rotate the camera to see how hair sits on the head from other angles. The preset hair is limited.

practice.title: Hair as volumes
practice.description: Draw heads and block hair into 3-5 big masses. No strands.

practice.title: Flow lines
practice.description: Mark the part and crown, then draw lines showing how hair falls from there.

practice.title: Hair types page
practice.description: For straight, wavy, curly, coily, braided and short hair, draw four thumbnails each.

practice.title: Light on hair
practice.description: Find the highlight band and the shadow shape on a lit head of hair; draw those first.

practice.title: Hair in motion
practice.description: Draw heads where hair reacts to wind or movement.

done_when: You can block in hair as volumes on any head construction.
Part and growth direction are clear in your drawings.
You can draw at least four hair types without them looking the same.
You add strand detail only where it helps.
common_mistakes: Drawing each strand as a line (the spaghetti look).
Putting hair flat on the skull with no volume.
Ignoring the hairline shape.
Using one hair type for every character.

title: Clothing and drapery folds
summary: Folds happen because of tension, gravity and the body underneath: sleeves and trousers wrap limbs, and cloth hangs from support points. You learn the main fold types, then draw clothed figures by building the body first. Hampton's free drapery lessons are the best free structured material; a public-domain figure book and a Met open-access drapery study add reading and copying.
learning_outcomes: Find tension points and gravity direction in a clothed pose and show them with fold lines.
Name and draw the main fold types (pipe, diaper, half-lock, spiral, compression, flag, inert).
Draw sleeve and trouser folds that follow the limb form.
Simplify busy cloth reference into a few big shapes.

The lesson Intro to Pipe Folds and Diaper Folds (19:07) is also marked free on its own page. The lesson A Review of the 7 Folds is premium.
resources.notes: Watch the free lessons in order: Introduction to Drapery, Drawing Gesture for Drapery, Figure Construction for Drapery, then Constructing the Back of the Figure, and the free 'Intro to Pipe Folds and Diaper Folds' (https://www.proko.com/course-lesson/intro-to-pipe-folds-and-diaper-folds). The review of the 7 folds is premium.

practice.title: Fold taxonomy sheet
practice.description: Using real cloth, draw each of the seven fold types on one page, labelled.

practice.title: Tension map
practice.description: Drape cloth on a chair arm or a hand. Mark tension points, then draw folds radiating from them.

practice.title: Body first, then cloth
practice.description: Construct a figure from gesture, then add a shirt and trousers that follow the limb forms.

practice.title: Real cloth study
practice.description: Hang a towel or shirt from one point and draw it. No tools needed.

practice.title: Master drapery copies
practice.description: Copy drapery studies from the Met's open-access works.

practice.title: Outfit thumbnails
practice.description: Reduce outfits to 3-5 shapes on a figure.

done_when: You can show where tension and gravity create the folds in a clothed pose.
You can name and draw at least five fold types.
Sleeves and trousers wrap around limbs rather than lie flat.
You can simplify a busy photo of cloth into big shapes.
common_mistakes: Random wrinkle lines with no cause.
Drawing clothes as flat stickers with no body underneath.
Too many folds, all the same weight.
Ignoring fabric type (stiff versus soft).

title: Figure in perspective and foreshortening
summary: Foreshortening is the squashing of a limb or torso as it points toward or away from you. You learn to use boxes, overlaps and size change instead of drawing the full length. Free structured lessons for the figure are thin, so this module combines Vandruff's perspective lessons, a rotating 3D pose tool and Muybridge's multi-view photos.
learning_outcomes: Draw a limb pointing at the viewer so it reads as short and close, using overlaps and size change.
Keep a consistent eye level across a whole figure.
Build a torso and limbs as boxes in 2-point perspective.
Find and fix foreshortening errors in your own sketches.

practice.title: Box people
practice.description: Draw the torso as a box and the limbs as boxes in perspective, in poses with a limb pointing at the viewer.

practice.title: Overlap and size
practice.description: Draw a limb pointing toward the viewer. Make the near end larger and overlap the rest.

practice.title: One pose, four cameras
practice.description: Pose a 3D figure and draw it from four camera heights.

practice.title: Tube ellipses
practice.description: Draw arm and leg tubes with contour ellipses curving toward the viewer.

practice.title: Phone and mirror
practice.description: Photograph your own arm pointing at the camera and draw it.

practice.title: Worm's-eye and bird's-eye
practice.description: Draw figures from extreme low and high viewpoints, with a horizon line.

done_when: A limb pointing at the viewer looks short and close, not stretched.
Eye level is consistent across the figure.
You can draw a torso and limbs as boxes in perspective.
You can spot a foreshortening error in a sketch and say why.
common_mistakes: Drawing the limb at full length.
Ignoring overlaps, so forms look pasted side by side.
Drawing parallel contour lines that flatten the form.
Using wide-angle photos, which exaggerate foreshortening.

title: Dynamic poses, action, interaction between two figures, weight and balance
summary: Dynamic poses show where weight sits, what is about to happen, and how two bodies share balance and rhythm. You practise finding the support leg and balance point, drawing action sequences, and linking two figures with one rhythm. Free two-person references are scarce, so some of this relies on your own photos and the school syllabus idea of a double-model pose.
learning_outcomes: Find the support leg and balance point in a pose and show the weight clearly.
Draw an off-balance pose that clearly falls, leaps or lunges.
Link two figures with a shared line of action and mark contact points.
Push a pose with a stronger line of action and clearer silhouette.

practice.title: Weight line
practice.description: Drop a vertical line from the pit of the neck and mark where it lands relative to the feet. See where the weight sits.

practice.title: Support leg
practice.description: Label which leg carries the weight and draw the hips and shoulders tilting in opposite directions.

practice.title: Action sequences
practice.description: Take a Muybridge sequence and draw a 1-minute gesture of each frame.

practice.title: Two-figure gesture
practice.description: Use photos of two people (dance, sport, hugging). Draw one line of action through both and mark contact points.

practice.title: Contact points
practice.description: In five two-figure poses, mark where the bodies touch and which figure carries the weight.

practice.title: Push the pose

done_when: You can find the support leg and balance point in any pose.
An off-balance pose clearly looks like it is falling or moving.
Two figures read as connected by one rhythm.
Your silhouettes are readable.
common_mistakes: Floating figures (feet not under the centre of mass).
Symmetrical standing poses.
Drawing two figures as separate stick people with no link.
Ignoring contact points and where weight goes.

title: Drawing the figure from imagination using a visual library
summary: Drawing without reference needs two things: a store of shapes and poses you have studied and can recall, and a construction habit that lets you rotate and combine them. You build the library by drawing from reference, hiding it, drawing from memory, and then checking. This is where George's characters, scenes and surreal ideas start to look solid.
learning_outcomes: Draw a believable figure in a pose you have not studied, using construction rather than reference.
Draw hands, feet and heads from memory at three angles.
Keep a visual library of at least 100 dated studies.
Make stylisation choices (elongate, simplify, exaggerate) on purpose.

resources.title: Constructive Anatomy (1920)
resources.free_notes: Archive.org shows 'Free Download, Borrow, and Streaming' (PDF and EPUB) for the 1920 Pelham, N.Y. edition and no rights statement. A 1920 US publication is public domain in the US; DrawingBooks.org states all its books are public domain in the US and shows the same book page by page at https://www.drawingbooks.org/bridgman1/index.html. Do not confuse it with Bridgman's later 1950s guides, which I did not check. The book contains anatomical drawings of nude figures.
resources.notes: Constructive Anatomy is a book of forms you can redraw from memory. Study a page, close it, redraw it from memory, check, and repeat for each region.

practice.title: Study, hide, draw
practice.description: Look at a reference for 60 seconds, hide it, draw from memory for 3 minutes, reveal and correct in a different colour.
practice.dose: 10 poses per session, twice a week

practice.title: Rotate it
practice.description: Draw a pose, then imagine turning it 90 degrees and draw that. Check with a 3D figure.

practice.title: Library pages
practice.description: Dedicate a sketchbook page to one subject (ribcages, hands, feet, twisting torsos) and fill it with 20 small studies from memory.

practice.title: Invent a character
practice.description: Design a character in three poses: silhouette, construction, simple form.

practice.title: Surreal mash-up
practice.description: Combine a human figure with a non-human form (tree, machine, animal), keeping the construction.

practice.title: Always check
practice.description: After every memory drawing, compare with reference and mark errors in a different colour.

done_when: You can draw a believable figure in a new pose from imagination in 10 minutes.
Hands, feet and heads from memory hold up at three angles.
You have a dated library of 100+ studies.
You can explain your stylisation choices.
common_mistakes: Expecting to draw from memory without studying first.
Skipping the reference check afterwards, so errors become habits.
Repeating one pose over and over.
Putting style ahead of structure.

title: Master studies from open-access collections (added module)
summary: Copying and analysing drawings by earlier artists teaches simplification, gesture and economy of line faster than most lessons. Several museums let you download high-resolution drawings free, and a few historic anatomy atlases are free too. This module gives a method for choosing, copying and writing a short critique.
learning_outcomes: Copy a drawing for structure and rhythm, not just outline.
Write a three-sentence note on what the master simplified and why.
Build a personal reference folder of hands, feet, drapery and heads from free sources.
Know which collections allow downloads and for what use.

resources.notes: Use the Open Access filter (showOnly=openAccess) and search for figure studies, hands, drapery and portrait drawings. Download a high-resolution file and print or load it next to your sheet.

common_mistakes: Copying the outline and missing the rhythm.
Choosing only famous pieces instead of rough studies.
Not noting the source and licence.
Copying without analysing.

practice.description: Five 30-second poses, four 1-minute, three 2-minute, two 5-minute and one 20-minute pose, then a 10-minute review.

practice.title: Long pose structure
practice.description: For one 30-60 minute pose, spend 5 minutes on gesture, 20 on construction, the rest on refining shapes.

You can say what you are working on each week.
You have tried at least one live class or a live online session.

Skipping review.
Using the same reference every time.
Switching focus every session.
